blocks.text: A yam plant, a mould growing on stale bread, a tapeworm in a goat's intestine and the student reading this page all need food. Yet only one of them makes its own. Nutrition is the study of who makes food and who has to find it.

blocks.markdown:
## Two great divisions

**Autotrophic nutrition** means the organism manufactures its own organic food from simple inorganic raw materials. There are two kinds:

- **Photosynthetic** — uses light energy. Green plants, algae and blue-green bacteria.
- **Chemosynthetic** — uses energy from chemical reactions. Certain bacteria, such as the nitrifying bacteria in soil.

**Heterotrophic nutrition** means the organism depends on ready-made organic food obtained from other organisms. Animals, fungi, most bacteria and a few non-green plants feed this way.

blocks.title: Parasite versus saprophyte
blocks.text: A parasite feeds on a living host and harms it. A saprophyte feeds on dead organic matter and harms nobody — indeed saprophytes are essential decomposers that return nutrients to the soil.

blocks.markdown:
### Food classes in a balanced diet

A **balanced diet** contains all the food classes in the right proportions for a person's age, sex and occupation.

Carbohydrates are the main source of energy; a gram of carbohydrate releases about 17 kJ. Fats and oils give more than twice as much energy per gram and also insulate the body. Proteins are the only class that supplies nitrogen for growth and repair, so a growing child and a pregnant woman need more. Mineral salts and vitamins are needed in small amounts to regulate body processes, and water and roughage complete the diet.

Roughage, or dietary fibre, is indigestible cellulose. It is not a nutrient at all, but it gives the gut wall something to grip, stimulating peristalsis and preventing constipation.

blocks.title: Diagnosing a nutritional deficiency
blocks.prompt: A two-year-old child in a rural community is fed almost entirely on garri and pap. The child has a swollen belly, thin arms and legs, pale reddish hair and sores on the skin. Which deficiency is this, and how should the diet be corrected?

steps.text: Identify what the diet supplies. Garri and pap are almost pure starch, so the child has a reasonable energy intake.
Identify what the diet lacks. Neither food contains appreciable protein, so protein intake is very low while energy intake is not.
Match the symptoms. Swollen abdomen caused by fluid retention (oedema), wasted limbs, changed hair colour and skin lesions with adequate calories is the classic picture of kwashiorkor.
Distinguish it from marasmus. In marasmus both energy and protein are lacking, the child is severely underweight and there is no oedema.
Correct the diet. Add cheap, locally available protein: beans, groundnut, crayfish, egg, milk, moringa or soya. Continue the energy foods so the protein is used for growth rather than burnt for fuel.

blocks.answer: The child has kwashiorkor, a protein deficiency. The diet must be supplemented with protein-rich foods such as beans, groundnut, crayfish, fish or egg.

blocks.title: Insectivorous plants are still autotrophic
blocks.text: Plants such as the sundew and pitcher plant trap insects, but they still photosynthesise. They digest the insect for its nitrogen and mineral salts, not for energy, because they grow in nitrogen-poor soils. So they are autotrophs with a supplement, not heterotrophs.

blocks.title: Naming deficiency diseases
blocks.text: Examiners want the disease name and the missing nutrient together. 'Goitre — iodine', 'scurvy — vitamin C', 'rickets — vitamin D', 'anaemia — iron', 'beriberi — vitamin B1', 'kwashiorkor — protein'. Learn them as pairs and the marks are automatic.

points: Autotrophs make organic food from inorganic materials, using light (photosynthesis) or chemical energy (chemosynthesis).
Heterotrophs use ready-made organic food and may be holozoic, saprophytic, parasitic or symbiotic.
A parasite harms its living host; a saprophyte feeds on dead matter; in symbiosis both partners benefit.
A balanced diet supplies carbohydrate, protein, fat, vitamins, mineral salts, water and roughage in suitable proportions.
Each deficiency disease is linked to one missing nutrient: kwashiorkor to protein, scurvy to vitamin C, rickets to vitamin D, goitre to iodine and anaemia to iron.
